title: React Fundamentals
description: Learn the React mental model from the ground up. Understand components, JSX syntax, props, and how React efficiently updates the UI. Build your first interactive UI components from scratch.
learningObjectives: Understand the React component model and virtual DOM
Write JSX and understand how it compiles to JavaScript
Pass and consume props including children
Understand component composition and prop drilling

lessons.title: What is React & The Component Model

sections.content: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Its key insight: break UI into small, reusable components — each responsible for its own appearance and behaviour. React efficiently updates only the parts of the DOM that change, using a virtual DOM diffing algorithm.
💡 React is not a full framework like Angular. It handles the View layer only. You pair it with tools like React Router (routing) and libraries like Zustand/Redux (state management).
🎯 Component names MUST start with a capital letter. <greeting /> is treated as an HTML element; <Greeting /> is a React component.

exercises.question: Why must React component names start with a capital letter?
options: It's a convention with no technical reason
React uses it to distinguish components from HTML elements
Lowercase causes a syntax error in JSX
Capital letters improve performance
exercises.correctAnswer: React uses it to distinguish components from HTML elements
exercises.explanation: In JSX, <div> compiles to React.createElement('div', ...) — a string. <MyComp> compiles to React.createElement(MyComp, ...) — a reference to your function. Capital letters tell the JSX compiler to treat it as a component.

exercises.question:
What is wrong with this JSX?
Hello
options: div is not a valid JSX element
class should be className in JSX
Hello must be wrapped in curly braces
Missing a closing tag
exercises.correctAnswer: class should be className in JSX
hints: class is a reserved word in JavaScript
exercises.explanation: class is a reserved JavaScript keyword (used for ES6 classes). JSX uses className instead. When compiled, className becomes the class attribute in the final HTML.

sections.content: Props (properties) are how you pass data into components. They flow one-way: parent → child. A component receives props as its first function argument — an object containing all the passed values.

exercises.question: If a component receives props but doesn't use a prop that was passed, what happens?
options: React throws an error
The prop is ignored silently
The component fails to render
TypeScript catches it at runtime
hints: React is permissive about extra props
exercises.explanation: React silently ignores props that are passed but not destructured or accessed by the component. No error is thrown. This is how optional props work — they're simply not used if not needed.

sections.content: The special children prop receives whatever is placed between a component's opening and closing tags. This enables powerful composition patterns — wrapper components like layouts, modals, and cards that display arbitrary content inside them.

exercises.question: What is the 'children' prop in React?
options: An array of all child components in the app
The content placed between a component's opening and closing tags
A list of nested HTML elements
React's internal state management
exercises.correctAnswer: The content placed between a component's opening and closing tags
hints: Think about how you nest HTML elements
exercises.explanation: children represents whatever JSX is placed between <Component>here</Component>. It can be text, elements, other components, or even functions — enabling composition-based patterns.

sections.content: ⚠️ Never use array index as key if the list can be reordered or filtered. Use a stable unique ID from your data. Index keys cause React to misidentify elements and produce bugs.

exercises.question: Why does React require a key prop when rendering lists?
options: It improves CSS styling of list items
It helps React identify which items changed, were added, or removed between renders
It's required by the JavaScript spec
It prevents duplicate components
exercises.correctAnswer: It helps React identify which items changed, were added, or removed between renders
hints: React needs to know which element is which during reconciliation
exercises.explanation: React uses keys to reconcile the virtual DOM with the actual DOM. Without keys, React re-renders the entire list on every change. With stable keys, it only updates the elements that actually changed.

capstoneProject.title: Component Library Showcase
capstoneProject.description: Build a component showcase page featuring 6 production-quality React components using only function components and props.
requirements: Button component (variant prop: primary/secondary/danger, size: sm/md/lg, disabled)
Card component with children prop for content composition
Badge component with color and label props
Avatar component with src, alt, size, and fallback initials
A CourseList that renders 6+ CourseCards from a data array using .map() with keys
All components are in separate files and exported correctly
